reason: Functional: a link to the contributing guide. The link's own text reads "Contribute", the icon is aria-hidden, and no alternative text was written for it.
Functional: the footer logo links to the site root. The alt describes the fleur de lis artwork instead of the destination, and misspells the university's name, which a screen reader will pronounce.

Functional: the main menu toggle. The label names the action and the icon is correctly aria-hidden. The inner spans are visually hidden, so there is no visible text for the announced name to contradict.

The alt says "Health Topics" while the link goes to Ebola travel guidance and the overlay text reads "Ebola Travel Updates". It misnames the destination, and the image itself is a photograph rather than a functional graphic.
Functional: a logo linking to another site's home page. Here the brand name is the destination, which is what makes it good, unlike a bare brand name on a link back to the current site's own root.
Functional: the next control of a carousel. The label names the action and the direction, and nothing adjacent repeats it.
Functional: a link to the migrated issue on GitHub. The image has no alt at all, and the announced name is the sentence of text beside it.
Functional: the logo links to the site root. The alt is the bare project name, with nothing to say the link goes home.
Functional: closes the image dialogue. The SVG is correctly aria-hidden and the visually hidden span carries the label, so no alternative text was written for the graphic.

Not functional: a photograph in an Instagram grid, linking to the post. The image conveys what it shows rather than standing for a function, and its alt is a decent informative description of exactly that.
Functional: the masthead links to the site root. The alt is the publication's name and does not say the link goes home.
Functional: the global navigation accordion. The button already displays "Explore" and the chevron carries no alternative text of its own.
Functional: a banner linking to the FSF membership form. The alt is the slogan on the banner, and the two sentences of text inside the same link already name the action, so the correct alt is empty.
Functional: a sponsor logo linking to that sponsor's site. The company name is the destination, so naming it is the right answer here in a way it would not be on a link back to this site's own root.
Functional: a sibling-store logo that hands the visitor over to Wayfair's home page, so it is a linked logo rather than a plain navigational link. The brand name is the destination.
Functional: advances the image gallery. The SVG is aria-hidden and the visually hidden span carries the label, so there is no alt text for the graphic to judge.

A photograph inside a play button, so not a functional graphic. The announced name concatenates "Play Video: " with a description of the singers, when what the control needs is the video's name. The aria-labelledby also points at an id that does not exist.
Functional: the logo links to the site root, and the alt says so in as many words. Destination over label, with no mention of the drawing.

Functional: an icon linking to the outbreaks page. But the overlay text in the same link already reads "Find the latest outbreak information from CDC", so the alt repeats it and the correct alt is empty.
Functional: a logo linking to archive.org. The organisation name would name the destination, but the alt appends "logo", which describes the image and is the pattern the criteria call poor.
Functional: a card linking to the About page. The gears icon carries no alt attribute at all, and the announced name comes from the heading and paragraph beside it.
Functional: a sibling-store logo handing the visitor over to AllModern's home page, so it is a linked logo. The brand name is the destination.
Same finding as fi-2174: a photograph inside a play button, with an announced name that joins "Play Video: " to a description of the band rather than naming what will play.

Functional: the logo links to the site root. The alt opens with the agency name and then transcribes the tagline and the stylised 24/7 mark as "CDC twenty four seven", which is visual detail a screen reader user has no use for.
Functional: advances the highlights carousel. The label names the action and what moves, which an arrow glyph cannot convey on its own.
Functional: a sponsor logo linking to that sponsor's site, where the company name is the destination. Same reasoning as fi-1723 on the same page.
Functional: opens the do-not-sell dialogue. The alt is the single word "Icon", which conveys nothing at all, and the button's own text already carries the label, so the correct alt is empty.
Functional: an icon-only link to the publication's Facebook page, labelled on the link because the SVG has no title. The service name is the destination, and nothing in the label describes the glyph.
Functional: a sibling-store logo handing the visitor over to Birch Lane's home page, so it is a linked logo. The brand name is the destination.
Functional: the logo links to the site's own root. The alt is the bare agency name, so a person hears who runs the site but not that the link goes home.
